1. Hot Salt Bluing  
   • Steel parts are immersed in a molten nitrate salt bath (typically potassium nitrate/sodium hydroxide) at 290–310 °C.  
   • A controlled oxidation produces a layer of magnetite (Fe₃O₄) that yields a deep, lustrous black finish.  

2. Cold Bluing  
   • Parts are treated at room temperature with acidic selenium- or nitrite-based bluing solutions.  
   • The chemicals react with the surface to produce a thin oxide film; primarily used for touch-ups or small components.  

3. Parkerizing (Phosphate Conversion Coating)  
   • Components are submerged in a heated (65–90 °C) solution of manganese or zinc phosphates.  
   • A microcrystalline phosphate layer forms, providing a matte gray finish and enhanced corrosion resistance.  

4. Hard Chrome Electroplating  
   • Steel surfaces serve as the cathode in a chromic acid-based electrolytic bath.  
   • A deposit of metallic chromium builds up, offering high hardness, wear resistance and a bright silver appearance.  

5. Cerakote (Polymer-Ceramic Coating)  
   • A thin, spray-on ceramic-enhanced polymer is applied and then baked (typically 120–200 °C).  
   • Results in a uniform, thin (20–80 µm) colored coating with excellent chemical, impact and abrasion resistance.
